Burnstate is a native Mac menu bar app for people who code with AI.

It shows your Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and Vercel AI Gateway limits, marks how much of each window has passed, and tells you when you'd run out at your current pace.

• Pace every limit against the clock, with a run-out forecast
• Answer Claude Code permission prompts and questions from a card
• See every session's tokens, cost and models, from local logs
• Cooldown: break reminders that count only time away
• Burn report: a year of AI coding usage, shared as one link
• Desktop widgets [...] No account, no analytics, no Burnstate server.

On the other hand, though it might just be my specific environment, I was periodically asked to re-enter my password.

## The most effective part was the depletion pace detection

This is the reason I wanted to write an article about it.

Immediately after installation, CodexBar displayed both my Claude session limit and weekly limit.  
At that point, 37 percent of the weekly limit remained.  
Up to this point, it's just a 'Oh, I see, that's how much is left' kind of thing.

What was interesting was what came next: it told me that my consumption pace was 25 percent higher than the baseline.  
In other words, even though the limit was scheduled to reset in 4 days and 8 hours, the calculation showed that if I continued at my current pace, it would be depleted in 1 day and 13 hours. [...] In my case, since I am on the side that heavily uses Claude and Codex on a daily basis,  
there was a clear benefit to keeping it running.

## Summary

CodexBar is a tool that quietly visualizes AI usage limits—something that is usually invisible but hits you hard when it runs out—right in your menu bar. It's free, and installation is a breeze with Homebrew.

For me, the deciding factor was that it doesn't just show the remaining amount, but also predicts depletion based on consumption pace. If you use Claude or Codex frequently, I think installing it once will change your perspective a little.

## FAQ (Frequently Asked Questions)

Q. Is CodexBar free?  
A. Yes. It is open-source under the MIT license and there are no fees. You can check it out in the GitHub repository. [...] The author is Peter Steinberger (@steipete).

OpenClaw author. He is someone who has recently released several tools related to AI development. CodexBar is open-source under the MIT license and is free of charge. The repository can be found at   
 CodexBar (GitHub).

## What problem does it solve in the first place?

When you use Claude or Codex for coding on a daily basis, managing usage limits can be a subtle headache.

Session-based limits, weekly limits, monthly limits. We don't usually keep track of how much of these we have left.

And it's always when you're focused on your work that you suddenly hit the limit and have to stop. When this happens right before a deadline or when you're in the zone, it really hurts.

| Tool | What you see | Where the login comes from |
 --- 
| Claude Code | Session, weekly, Sonnet, and Fable limits, extra usage in your billing currency, banked resets | Claude Code's saved login |
| Codex | Session, weekly, and Spark limits, credits, banked resets | Codex's ChatGPT login |
| Cursor | Total, Auto, and API usage, on-demand spend | Cursor's login |
| Antigravity | Gemini session and weekly limits, Argon, Claude pool | Antigravity's Google login, or the running app or `agy` |
| GitHub Copilot | Credits, chat, and completions | Copilot's editor sign-in or the GitHub CLI |
| Devin | Daily and weekly quota | Devin's login |
| Grok | Weekly quota | Grok CLI's login |
| Kiro | Credits, free-trial credits, and overage spend | Kiro's or `kiro-cli`'s sign-in, or `KIRO_API_KEY` | [...] Track every tool you use and choose exactly what reaches the menu bar. Usage refreshes every 1, 5, 15, 30, or 60 minutes, and the refresh button works any time.

 How the menu bar decides what to show

 Weekly is selected for Claude Code and Codex at first, and Left is the default number mode.
 When a selected limit is missing, such as Claude's session window on accounts that have none, the tool's default limit is shown instead.
 The panel lists when each banked reset expires and turns the next one orange in its final 24 hours.
 Percentages are shown exactly as the provider reports them. Only the bars are clamped to `0...100`, and a remaining percentage never goes below zero.
